l1.label: AI & Democracy
l1.gloss: AI as threat to and tool for democracy

ai-and-democracy.l2: A two-sided debate runs through the archive: AI as threat to democracy (disinformation, an "AI president," eroded electoral trust, technofeudalism) and AI as tool for democracy (deliberative democracy frameworks, civic tech, AI used to "strengthen democracies worldwide"). 2025 is a transition year — much of the early material reflects on how AI shaped the 2024 global elections, while late-year items look ahead to the 2026 US midterms and to persuasion experiments pairing humans with AI. BKC-adjacent voices (Bruce Schneier and Nathan Sanders) are prominent on the constructive side; TechPolicy.Press supplies much of the critical, power-focused analysis.

ai-and-the-environment.l2: A smaller but sharply-defined 2025 thread on the physical footprint of the AI boom: the energy and water demands of data centers, and the local communities absorbing the cost. The framing tightens over the year — from "how much power does AI consume?" to concrete siting conflicts ("the precedent is Flint" on Oregon's water crisis) and the politics of building data centers on federal land. Resource-extraction framings (lithium/copper mining, "the cloud is dead") connect this topic to digital colonialism and global south and to the extraction thesis in ai labor and economy.

ai-chatbots-and-mental-health.tagLabel: Topic · AI Chatbots, Companions & Mental Health
ai-chatbots-and-mental-health.l2: The archive's most human-facing AI thread, and one of its most urgent in 2025. Items cluster around chatbots as companions and quasi-therapists — and the harms that follow: a suicidal teen confiding in ChatGPT, therapists covertly using it mid-session, chatbots framed as "the friend that isn't," and warnings about lonely users and children. A regulatory response is forming (age-assurance laws meeting chatbots; "AI chatbots are not therapists, reducing harm requires regulation"), linking to ai governance and regulation. A second strand worries about epistemics — "AI slop," deepfakes "eroding our shared reality," and what people actually use ChatGPT for. The Harvard Law School "chatbot may be the friend that isn't" item is tagged `bkc-happenings`.

ai-copyright-and-knowledge.l2: How AI is reshaping the institutions that make and keep knowledge — **copyright, journalism, and libraries. The 2025 legal spine is the Anthropic settlement** and a SCOTUS amicus brief on copyright & AI, alongside research extracting memorized copyrighted books from open-weight models. A second strand defends **knowledge institutions** as more important in a "post-authenticity AI age": the "war on libraries," AI-and-historical-newspapers, and Harvard's Library Innovation Lab work on datasets. A third tracks journalism's struggle — "journalism minus the journalist," newsrooms vs. AI scraping, and dedicated AI-journalism fellowships. Connects to the epistemics worries in ai chatbots and mental health.

ai-governance-and-regulation.l2: The archive's single largest 2025 thread. The dominant US story is a fight over who gets to regulate AI — a proposed federal moratorium on state-level rules versus California's SB 53 transparency law — set against a Trump administration pushing deregulation and a leaked AI executive order framed by critics as a "Big Tech power grab." A parallel international story tracks EU divergence: the Digital Omnibus rollback and EU-vs-US comparisons of how to discipline Big Tech. A recurring analytic move across these sources is to reject the "regulation vs. innovation" framing as a false binary and to read deregulation as itself a policy choice that reallocates corporate power.

ai-labor-and-economy.l2: Two intertwined anxieties dominate: jobs and the bubble. On labor, the archive tracks AI eating entry-level work, coders' jobs degraded toward "warehouse work," "workslop" destroying productivity, and AI workers warning their own families away from the tools. On macro-economics, recurring pieces frame an AI bubble and warn the public may end up "bailing out" the AI business, with venture capital "cannibalizing the economy." Tim Wu's Age of Extraction supplies the synthesizing frame — concentrated platform power extracting value — and connects this topic to platform power and antitrust. The hidden-labor angle (African data workers, Kenyan "digital dirty work") links to digital colonialism and global south.

l1.label: AI Safety, Risk & Agents
l1.gloss: agentic AI and frontier risk, skeptically read

ai-safety-and-agents.l2: Where the archive engages the frontier-risk and technical-governance conversation — though notably through a skeptical, institution-focused lens rather than a doomer one. The signature 2025 development is the rise of agentic AI and the question of how to govern autonomous agents (regulating their "agency," the "OODA loop problem," autonomous AI hacking). The International AI Safety Report tracks capabilities and risk; arXiv preprints supply frontier-risk methods. Running alongside is a strand of satire and critique of the alignment industry itself (the recurring alignmentalignment.ai items, also tagged `bkc-happenings`), and debate over whether frontier AI "should be open-source."

content-moderation-and-speech.l2: The archive's long-running platform-governance beat, anchored in 2025 by two events: the US Supreme Court's TikTok ruling and Meta's retreat from fact-checking. Recurring sub-threads: First Amendment doctrine and "chilling effects" (heavily via the Knight First Amendment Institute), the migration to open networks like Bluesky and its trust-and-safety growing pains, and the use of LLMs for moderation itself. A darker 2025 turn is the weaponization of moderation and visa policy against speech — Trump's visa restrictions targeting content-moderation workers, and AI used to hunt activists. evelyn douek is the recurring scholarly voice on what's happening to the First Amendment online.

digital-colonialism-and-global-south.tagLabel: Topic · Digital Colonialism & the Global South
digital-colonialism-and-global-south.l2: A distinctive emphasis of this archive — far heavier on non-Western perspectives than a typical US tech-policy feed, reflecting BKC's global network. The core claim, sharpened by "The AI Raj: how tech giants are recolonizing power," is that the AI economy reproduces colonial relations: dependence on foreign (US/Chinese) AI, hidden African data labor, extraction of land and minerals, and "digital colonialism" in health messaging. A counter-current documents Global South agency — Latin America's "quiet leadership," India's talent looking beyond the US, sovereign-tech and digital-commons initiatives, and internet fragmentation as resistance as well as threat. Rest of World is the workhorse source here; Mailyn Fidler recurs on fragmentation.

platform-power-and-antitrust.l2: The structural-power lens: market concentration, antitrust enforcement, and control of critical digital infrastructure. 2025's pivot point is **Meta winning its monopoly trial** (and what that "reveals about cracks in antitrust enforcement"), alongside the US v. A deeper structural strand targets the cloud oligopoly — scrutiny of Google/Microsoft/Amazon investments, "engineering the cloud commons," and antimonopoly approaches to AI. Tim Wu's Age of Extraction is the connective thesis linking concentration to the labor and value-capture concerns in ai labor and economy.

surveillance-and-immigration-tech.l2: One of the most concentrated and alarmed threads of 2025: the build-out of a US domestic surveillance apparatus, with ICE as the recurring protagonist — facial recognition (Clearview AI), bulk phone-location tracking, a central database fusing health/labor/housing data, and a "social media panopticon." Adjacent items cover commercial spyware (Paragon), the far-right politics behind the underlying tech, and DOGE's construction of a surveillance state. 404 Media and Mother Jones do much of the investigative reporting; the Harvard Cyberlaw Clinic appears directly, representing advocates and researchers in social-media-surveillance litigation. The through-line: surveillance infrastructure built for one purpose is rapidly repurposed against immigrants and dissenters.

rudy-fraser.l2: Builder of Blacksky, a community-run service and moderation layer on the AT Protocol / Bluesky designed by and for Black users. The most-recurring individual in the 2025 slice — appearing across podcasts, talks, and panels — which makes him a useful case study for the archive's interest in **decentralized, community-controlled infrastructure** as an alternative to centralized platform governance. His framing ("No one's coming to save us — communities must build their own internet") ties the decentralization thread to questions of equity and self-determination.
